title: The Tide Returns a Letter
subtitle: The Shore I Choose · Chapter 11 · Lanternweald continuation
content:
Three days after the lantern festival, the tide brought me a letter I had apparently written to myself.

It arrived in a cracked glass bottle, caught between two rocks where the beach narrowed below the old mooring post. I would have walked past it if Maui had not been arguing with a crab.

The crab had a scrap of festival ribbon in one claw. Maui wanted it back.

“It's the principle,” he told me when I stopped to watch.

“The principle that a crab can't decorate its home?”

“The principle that it stole from a demigod.”

“You left the ribbon on a rock.”

“A demigod's rock.”

The crab disappeared into a crevice with the ribbon, ending negotiations on terms of its own choosing. Maui looked personally betrayed.

That was when I spotted the bottle.

It was no longer clear glass. Sand had worn it milky, and a line of blue thread caught at the neck like a tiny flag. I crouched, slid it free, and turned it over in my hands. A folded sheet of paper lay inside. The cork had held despite a thin crack running down one side.

Maui leaned over my shoulder.

“Treasure?”

“Probably a shopping list.”

“Those can be treasure if you're hungry.”

The paper slid out with some persuasion. It smelled of damp salt and old ink. At the top, in handwriting that made the base of my skull tighten, stood a word.

JASPER.

Below it was a diagram of Tideglass Cove, the rocks, and three points farther out to sea. The little brass key I still wore around my neck had been drawn beside the third point.

My stomach dropped.

Maui noticed before I said anything. For once he did not turn concern into a joke.

“Is it yours?”

“I don't know.”

Then I looked again. I made the same odd slant on my capital letters. I put small boxes around numbers when they mattered. The diagram was careful in a way my hands remembered even when my mind refused to supply the past.

“I think it is,” I whispered.

Maui reached toward the page, stopped, and pulled his hand back.

“Can I see?”

I handed it over.

The writing beneath the map was nearly gone. Only two sentences remained legible.

*If the second tide comes in, mark the safe path before you try to close the door.*

*No one has to carry the sea alone.*

I read them twice.

They were not an answer to who I used to be. They were instructions. Practical, irritatingly specific instructions. I felt a strange mixture of disappointment and relief.

“I'm beginning to think I left myself paperwork instead of memories,” I said.

Maui studied the lines. “You were clearly a very exciting person.”

“I might have been an accountant.”

“A terrifying profession. They can defeat kings with numbers.”

I tried to laugh. It came out thin.

He gave the paper back.

“You want to know where it came from?”

“Yes.”

“Then we'll find out.”

“No, Maui. I want to find out. You can help. There is a difference.”

He looked at me, startled. Then his mouth moved into a reluctant smile.

“Right. We learned that one with the boulder.”

“We did.”

“Still think the boulder would've looked impressive.”

“Until the entire harbor disappeared.”

“Minor detail.”

We carried the letter to Neri, who was repairing a lamp outside the common kitchen. The festival bunting still hung between the arches. Nobody had agreed who was responsible for taking it down, so it had become a municipal feature.

Neri held the damp page by two dry corners.

“This is a sounding chart,” they said. “Not a letter.”

“It has my name on it.”

“Charts can have names.”

“It's from before I arrived.”

Neri studied the three marks past the reef. Their expression changed.

“Those are old water measurements. Before the Tideglass Door was braced properly, the inlet would sometimes pull against the outer current. We thought it was seasonal.”

“Was it?”

“We never had enough measurements to say.”

Maui folded his arms. “You had a mystery and didn't tell the magnificent expert standing right here?”

“You weren't standing here then,” Neri said. “You were arguing with a crab.”

Maui looked wounded all over again.

Neri pointed to the smallest mark. “A second tide means water surging into the cove from two directions. If that happens, the safest thing is to close the lower crossing until we understand the pressure.”

“So we need to check the anchors.”

“Yes. But please don't open a door to test whether it fails.”

I looked at Maui.

He held up both hands. “I was thinking something completely different.”

“You were thinking about opening it.”

“Briefly.”

We walked the shore that afternoon with a measuring line, a chalk board, and a basket of pegs. It was almost insultingly ordinary. No monsters. No great prophecy. Just cold water up to my calves and sand finding places sand had no business being.

I liked it.

At the third point from the chart, I found a groove cut into a flat stone. It was the exact width of my brass key.

I stared at it.

“Do you want to try?” Maui asked.

I traced the groove with one finger. A memory brushed against me: a hand tightening a blue cord, somebody laughing behind me, the smell of wet wood. Nothing more.

“Not yet.”

“All right.”

I looked up. “That's it?”

“I'm practicing.”

“You're very talented.”

“Finally, recognition.”

His grin was familiar. The patience beneath it was newer.

We marked the point and left the stone untouched. A choice postponed was still a choice.

By evening the lanterns along the cove came on one by one. The little spring beneath Lanternwell Square glimmered through the arch above us. Beyond the other doors, entire lives continued without knowing I had found a bottle.

Maui sat beside me on the dock, knees drawn up, hook resting against the railing. Even sitting, he occupied an unreasonable amount of space.

“You'll go through those doors,” he said.

“Probably.”

“You might meet people who matter to you.”

“I hope so.”

He nodded once, watching his reflection fracture on the water.

“We talked about that,” I said. “About how I prefer polyamory. About being honest even when a thing is uncomfortable.”

“I remember.”

“I don't want you to think leaving for a day means I've stopped choosing you.”

“I don't,” he said. Then, after a pause, “I might have to remind myself.”

“That makes two of us.”

He gave me a sideways look. “You too?”

“I'm afraid of people deciding they know who I am better than I do. Even when they love me.”

Maui set his hand on the dock between us, palm up.

“Then I'll ask,” he said. “And if I forget, you can hit me with a very small fish.”

“Why a small one?”

“I have a reputation.”

I took his hand.

The wood beneath us was warm from the day's sun. I could feel the roughness of his palm, the calluses made by rope and hook, the slight tremble he hoped I wouldn't notice. He turned his hand over and brushed the back of mine with his thumb.

“May I kiss you?” he asked, quieter than usual.

“You may.”

He leaned carefully toward me, and for once his size was not the thing that filled the space. It was the attention. The way he watched my face for permission to come closer. The way his smile slipped when I touched his cheek and returned when I kissed him.

When we drew apart, he rested his forehead against mine.

“Still here?” he asked.

“Still here.”

“Good.”

We stayed on the dock until the first stars appeared. Then we went back toward the little house above the cove, carrying the chart safely rolled inside my coat. I left the lantern burning by the window. The rest of the evening belonged to us.

I woke early to a hard tapping at the glass.

Rain.

Except the sky above Tideglass Cove was clear.

Farther uphill, six threshold lamps glimmered under an invisible drizzle. A bead of water ran down the inside of the Moonroot lamp's brass frame and fell onto the stone.

The ink on Neri's maintenance board had begun to blur.

I stood in the doorway, the old chart in my hand, and understood exactly why somebody had once thought to write instructions about a second tide.

This time, I would not be measuring alone.
